newsitem.title: JAPAN: Nomura directors in "apparently irregular" deal.
newsitem.headline: Nomura directors in "apparently irregular" deal.

text.p: Japan's Nomura Securities Co Ltd said on Thursday that two of its directors had been involved in an "apparently irregular" deal with a corporate client.

Nomura vice president Atsushi Saito told a hastily called news conference that Japan's securities watchdog was now investigating stock transactions which he said two Nomura directors made through the client's account several times without approval from the client.

"We are sorry to say this, but we found transactions which are regarded as discretionary," Saito said, adding that discretionary deals are transactions made without a customer's approval and are "irregular" and against the Securities and Exchange Law.
"The Securities and Exchange Surveillance Commission (SESC) investigation is continuing and Nomura is cooperating," Saito said.
Saito added that the company discovered the transactions after starting its own checks at the beginning of the year.
The client's account was set up in early 1993, Saito said.
Saito said the two directors also appeared to have transferred profits raised from Nomura's own funds to the customer's account. He said this was also an "apparently irregular" action.
"We apologise that we betrayed the public trust," he said.

Saito said those deals had been made at the directors' own judgement and the company itself had not been involved in the case. Nomura submitted a report about the case to the SESC in February, he said.

Asked if the client was a "sokaiya" -- that is, a firm involved in corporate racketeering -- Saito said he could not confirm that at the moment. But he said the client had a long-time relationship with the directors and had a family connection to a Nomura shareholder.

Saito also said the SESC was expected to unveil its formal decision on the issue sometime later, but did not give any likely timing. He said Nomura plans to take punitive measures against the directors involved.
"We will wait for a final outcome of the SESC's investigation," he said. Nomura would work out measures to avoid any recurrence of such shaky deals, he said.

Last September, a report carried by a regional Japanese newspaper said Nomura officials were being investigated by the watchdog on suspicion that the company had reimbursed huge sums to a Tokyo-based corporate investor to make up for losses incurred through futures trading in Singapore.
Nomura at that time denied that the probe had been conducted into the actions of its officials.

Japanese media have reported that the top Japanese brokerage firm was suspected of having provided, through trading in bank shares, undue profits of tens of millions of yen to an company run by a relative of a an unidentified "sokaiya".
